text: Imagine a time in the near future when you are driving on the highway in a self-driving car. You are surrounded by other cars when suddenly, a large, heavy object falls from a truck in front of you. Your car cannot stop in time, so it must make a decision: go straight and hit the object, ____ (move quickly to the side) left into an SUV, or swerve right into a motorcycle.

Should the car ____ (give more importance to) your safety by hitting the motorcycle? Should it avoid swerving, even if that means crashing into the object and ____ (giving up) your life? Or should it hit the SUV, which is designed to protect passengers well? What is the right choice?

If a person were driving, their reaction would be natural and ____ (based on feeling rather than careful thought). But if a programmer tells the car how to react in this situation, it seems like a planned decision rather than an accident.

Self-driving cars are expected to reduce accidents by removing human mistakes. They may also help with traffic, reduce pollution, and make driving less stressful. However, accidents will still happen. When they do, the outcome may have already been decided by programmers or ____ (people who make rules for society).

For example, imagine the same situation, but now there are two motorcyclists: one wearing a helmet and one without. Which one should the car hit? If it crashes into the one with a helmet because they are more likely to survive, is that fair? It seems like the responsible rider is being ____ (punished unfairly). But if the car avoids the helmeted rider and crashes into the one without a helmet, it is no longer just minimizing harm—it is making a moral ____ (a difficult choice between two options).
In both examples, the car’s programming acts like a ____ (a system that finds and selects something). It chooses who will suffer, even though the victims did nothing wrong.
New technology creates many difficult ethical questions.

For instance, if you had to buy a car, would you choose one that always tries to save the most lives, or one that always protects you first? What if the car could analyze people inside the vehicles and make decisions based on their lives? Would that be fair? Or would a ____ (not planned, decided by chance) decision be better? And who should make these rules—programmers, companies, or governments?

Real life may not play out exactly like these examples, but that is not the point. These thought experiments help us understand ethical problems, just as science experiments help us understand the physical world. Thinking about these issues now will help us ____ (move through something difficult) the future of technology and make better decisions along the way.
